seoTitle: How to Embed a PDF in an Outlook Email Body
metaDescription: Embed a PDF directly in an Outlook message as an inline icon using the Object insertion tool — and why it only works in classic Outlook for Windows, in Rich Text format.
intro:
A standard attachment sitting up in the header can easily get overlooked in a busy or long email thread. Outlook's Object insertion tool lets you place a PDF directly inside your message text as an interactive icon instead, right at the point in the paragraph where it belongs.

Two things need to be true before this works the way most guides describe it: you need classic Outlook for Windows, and your message needs to be in Rich Text format, not HTML. This guide covers both, then walks through the Insert tab's Object wizard to drop the file inline.
prerequisites: Classic Outlook for Windows (the traditional desktop app) — Insert > Object isn't available in new Outlook, Outlook on the web, or Outlook for Mac
The message format set to Rich Text, since the Display as icon option this guide relies on doesn't appear when composing in HTML

steps.heading: Start a new message
steps.body: Click New mail to open a fresh compose window, which uses the ribbon-based Message tab by default. That tab holds formatting controls, the address book, and a condensed Insert group for attaching files or pictures quickly. It's fine for a standard attachment, but it isn't where the full Object insertion tool lives. For that you need the dedicated Insert tab covered in the next step, not the shortcut icons sitting on Message.

image.caption: A new, blank compose window on the Message tab, with the To field active and a suggested contact showing above the subject line.

steps.heading: Switch your message format to Rich Text
steps.body: Object insertion itself works in HTML-format messages, but the Display as icon checkbox this whole guide depends on only appears when the message is formatted as Rich Text. Skip this step and Outlook will still let you insert the PDF, just as a large embedded preview instead of the compact icon this guide is after. Check the current mode under the Format Text tab in the ribbon, in the Format group on the far left, and switch it to Rich Text before continuing.

steps.heading: Position your cursor and open the Insert tab
steps.body: Click into the body of the email at the exact line where you want the file to sit. This matters because whatever you insert next anchors to that cursor position, not to the top or bottom of the message. With the cursor placed, switch from Message to the Insert tab along the top ribbon, which exposes a fuller set of insertion tools than the condensed group on Message, including Pictures, Shapes, Charts, and further along, Object.

steps.heading: Launch the Object wizard and choose your file
steps.body: In the Text group toward the right of the Insert tab, click the Object icon to open the insertion dialog. Switch to the Create from File tab instead of the default Create New tab, since you're embedding an existing document, not building one from scratch. Click Browse, navigate to your PDF, and select it. The file path populates a text field in the dialog, confirming what's about to be embedded.

steps.heading: Display it as a compact icon
steps.body: Before confirming, check Display as icon on the right side of the Object dialog. This box only shows up because the message is in Rich Text format; if it's missing, go back and check the format from the previous step. With it checked, the PDF appears as a small, clickable icon positioned exactly where your cursor was, instead of a large preview stacked wherever Outlook decides to render it. An optional Change Icon button lets you customize the label shown underneath if the default filename isn't descriptive enough.

steps.heading: Finish and verify the layout
steps.body: Click OK to drop the icon into your message, then click around it to confirm you can still type text immediately before and after it without the layout breaking. This is worth a quick check, since inline objects occasionally interact oddly with existing formatting, especially inside bulleted lists or tables. If this is the first time you've used the feature, send yourself a test copy so you can confirm the icon opens the PDF correctly on the receiving end instead of just trusting it locally.

troubleshooting.problem: There's no Object button anywhere on the Insert tab
troubleshooting.cause: Object insertion is a classic Outlook for Windows feature. It isn't included in new Outlook for Windows, Outlook on the web, or Outlook for Mac.
troubleshooting.fix: Open the message in classic Outlook for Windows instead. If your organization has already moved everyone to new Outlook, a normal file attachment or a cloud storage link is the closest available alternative.

troubleshooting.problem: The Display as icon checkbox is missing or grayed out in the Object dialog
troubleshooting.cause: The message is composed in HTML format. That checkbox is only available in Rich Text.
troubleshooting.fix: Close the dialog, switch the message format under Format Text > Format > Rich Text, then reopen Insert > Object.

troubleshooting.problem: The inserted PDF shows as a large preview instead of a small icon
troubleshooting.cause: The object was inserted before switching to Rich Text, or Display as icon was left unchecked.
troubleshooting.fix: Delete the inserted object, confirm the message is in Rich Text format, and reinsert it with Display as icon checked this time.

faq.question: Why don't I see an Object option on my Insert tab at all?
faq.answer: You're likely in new Outlook, Outlook on the web, or Outlook for Mac. Inline object embedding is a classic Outlook for Windows feature and isn't available in those versions.

faq.question: Why is Display as icon grayed out or missing?
faq.answer: Your message format needs to be Rich Text, set under the Format Text tab. Display as icon doesn't appear at all in HTML or Plain Text messages.

faq.question: Can I change the icon or label shown for the file?
faq.answer: Yes. The Change Icon option inside the Object dialog lets you customize the text label displayed underneath the icon before you confirm.

faq.question: What happens when the recipient clicks the embedded icon?
faq.answer: They double-click the icon directly in the body text to open the file, instead of downloading it separately from a header attachment list.

faq.question: Should I use this method for very large files?
faq.answer: For files over about 20 megabytes, a cloud storage link is generally a better option than embedding directly, since large embedded objects can bloat the message and trigger size limits.

faq.question: Is the Object tool the same as just attaching a file normally?
faq.answer: No. A normal attachment sits in the header above the message body, while the Object tool anchors the file inline at your cursor position inside the text itself.

verifiedNote: Click path and screens come from a walkthrough recorded in classic Outlook for Windows. Re-checked against Microsoft's official support documentation in September 2026, which corrected two things this guide previously got wrong: Display as icon requires Rich Text format specifically, not 'HTML or Rich Text' as stated before, and the Object insertion tool itself is limited to classic Outlook for Windows, absent from new Outlook, Outlook on the web, and Outlook for Mac.
